claims.text: HfZrTiTa0.53 has a reported yield strength of approximately 786 MPa.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has a reported compressive strength of approximately 1314 MPa.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has a reported terminal compressive strain of approximately 13.5%.
Baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 has limited tensile ductility.
Baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 exhibits high impact-triggered energy release.
The proposed intervention is addition of approximately 1–2 atomic % Al to HfZrTiTa0.53 during melt processing.
Post-alloying annealing will facilitate precipitate formation.
Al addition and annealing will produce a refined microstructure containing coherent nanoscale Al-rich precipitates along grain boundaries.
The proposed Al-rich precipitates will pin grain boundaries.
The proposed precipitates will impede dislocation motion and help refine the grain structure.
Precipitate-induced microstructural refinement and dislocation obstruction will delay plastic-strain localization.
Delayed strain localization will promote more uniform plastic deformation during tensile loading.
Al modification will increase tensile ductility and uniform elongation by at least 30–50% relative to the unmodified alloy.
The modified alloy's compressive strength will remain statistically unchanged relative to unmodified HfZrTiTa0.53.
The modified alloy's impact-triggered energy release will remain statistically unchanged relative to unmodified HfZrTiTa0.53.
The hypothesis is limited to room-temperature tensile and compression testing at approximately 10^-3 s^-1.
The hypothesis assumes that Al addition and annealing do not cause detrimental phase transformations or significant embrittlement.

contradictions.description: The conditions field distinguishes quasistatic tension/compression from impact testing under prior impact conditions, whereas the experimental design can be read as placing compression, tension, and impact penetration tests all under quasistatic conditions. An impact penetration test is not consistently specified as quasistatic.
